title: Plant branching patterns come from simple substitution-system growth rules

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Plant branching patterns come from simple substitution-system growth rules

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The overall branching patterns of plants, from algae to ferns to trees and flowering plants, are produced by simple growth rules in which each stem tip repeatedly splits into smaller copies of itself at fixed relative lengths and angles.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And no doubt it is from such simple rules of growth that most such overall branching patterns come.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 8, “Implications for Everyday Systems”; section “Growth of Plants and Animals” (from p. 400), p. 401. Scope: overall branching architecture of plants

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch08-19: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.60

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Plant architecture and recursive-model parameters are measurable, and existing repositories cover some taxa. They do not provide uniform time-resolved developmental data across algae, ferns, trees, and flowering plants. Model fit alone also has limited power to establish the actual growth mechanism.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit recursive fixed-angle, fixed-ratio branching models to time-resolved and mature plant architectures across major lineages, then compare held-out geometry with models allowing nonrecursive developmental control and environmental plasticity. Systematic predictive success with few fixed parameters would support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Branching responds strongly to light, damage, hormones, and resource gradients.

Public data emphasize mature form rather than repeated tip-splitting trajectories.

Most overall patterns spans very different plant lineages.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.48
discriminating power: 0.58
analysis feasibility: 0.55
data existence: 0.72
operationalizability: 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Branching geometry can be compared with substitution-system output, and public images and trait compilations cover many growth forms. The compilations are thin on the actual angles and length ratios, and a successful fit does not discriminate the developmental mechanism from other branching models. The claim is testable as a geometric description for a subset of plants.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit fixed-angle, fixed-length-ratio branching rules to measured plant architectures from algae through woody plants, and compare them with alternative growth rules on held-out geometry. A small family of substitution rules that recovers most branching topologies would support the claim; systematic residuals that require other mechanisms would refute it for those taxa.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A geometric fit does not show that the apex uses that substitution rule rather than auxin-mediated branching.

Trait databases record size and leaves more often than full branching angles and length ratios.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.55
discriminating power: 0.5
data adequacy: 0.45
analysis feasibility: 0.55
operationalizability: 0.65
